sections.heading: Giannis D – Abu Nuhas
sections.text: : In 26m of water and leaning to port with a fully intact stern section and an impressive engine room packed with glassfish.

sections.heading: Carnatic – Abu Nuhas:
sections.text: A British P&O steamer which struck the reef in 1869. She lays in 29m and now the whole hull is draped in multicolored soft corals. The wreck is home to glassfish, octopus, morays, jacks, and tuna cruise overhead.

sections.heading: Big Brother Island:
sections.text: A 400-meter long island offering fabulous wreck diving and wall diving. The wreck of the Numidia lies on the northern tip between 10 and 80 meters. The northwest side of the island houses the wreck of the Aida. Every section of this reef is covered with corals and life.

sections.heading: Little Brother Island:
sections.text: From its name, you can guess that it is a little smaller than Big Brother Island! It is surrounded by walls, covered in soft corals. The dives can be challenging but are definitely rewarding. Sightings of large pelagic are very common and the beautiful Gorgonia Fan coral forest is an awe-inspiring sight.

sections.heading: Small Crack:
sections.text: This is a small split in the middle of Shaab Mahmoud’s barrier. Drift along the outside wall next to beautiful corals and colorful fish. Look for a sand slope that leads you up and through the crack. When the current is right you can fly through the 5m deep channel and be thrown out across the sandy lagoon!

sections.heading: Gubal Island:
sections.text: At the gate of the Straits of Gubal is ‘Bluff Point’, which gets its name from the turbulence created by strong currents that beat the eastern wall of the island. The wreck of the ‘Ulysses’ lies on the reef 300m north of the lighthouse, starting at 5m and sloping to 25m. ‘The Barge’ wreck, south of the lighthouse, provides divers with a fun and unusual night dive. The wrecks skeleton creates protection for all types of night creatures.

sections.heading: Marine Life:
sections.text: Wrecks, rays, sharks, octopus, lionfish, nudibranchs, frogfish, huge schools of fish, bright colorful reefs. All dive sites are subject to weather conditions and the final route taken is at the absolute discretion of the captain and dive guides.

blue::North & Tiran (Hurghada - Hurghada.name: North & Tiran (Hurghada - Hurghada)
blue::North & Tiran (Hurghada - Hurghada.experience: Open Water - 30 minimum logged dives required.
blue::North & Tiran (Hurghada - Hurghada.intro: Similar to the Northern & Ras Mohamed itinerary, the Strait of Tiran and North cruise allows you to take in some of the most notorious wrecks and reefs the Red Sea has to offer as well as the pristine coral reefs of Tiran. The Tiran dive area is found in the entrance to the Gulf of Aqaba and is made up of four main reefs that form the top of an underwater bridge. These reefs, named after British cartographers (Jackson, Woodhouse, Thomas, Gordon), are world-famous for their extraordinary diversity of corals and strong south westerly currents make them home to many large pelagic fish.

sections.heading: SS. Thistlegorm – Shaab Ali:
sections.text: Probably the most famous of the Red Sea wrecks. The 129m English Freighter was bombed by German aviation on 6th October 1941. Today she creates an artificial reef on a sandy bottom at 32m max depth. She is home to an enormous variety of marine life and is especially popular with large schooling fish.

sections.heading: Small Crack – Shaab Mahmoud:
sections.text: This is a small split in the middle of Shaab Mahmoud’s barrier. Drift along the outside wall next to beautiful corals and colorful fish. Look for a sand slope that leads you up and through the crack. When the current is right you can fly through the 5m deep channel and be thrown out across the sandy lagoon!

sections.heading: Shag Rock:
sections.text: This large circular reef is often overlooked but offers excellent diving on pristine coral from any location on its perimeter.

sections.heading: Abu Nuhas:
sections.text: Also known as the ‘Ships Graveyard’, this reef is dangerously positioned close to the busy shipping lanes of the Gulf of Suez. This reef has claimed more ships than any other in the area. On the north side are four wrecks laying on a sandy seafloor at the bottom of a steep sloping reef layered with table corals. On the south side is a safe anchorage for liveaboards and two ergs, known as Yellow Fish Reef.

sections.heading: Marine Life:
sections.text: Wrecks, rays, sharks, octopus, lionfish, nudibranchs, frogfish, huge schools of fish, bright colorful reef. All dive sites are subject to weather conditions and the final route taken is at the absolute discretion of the captain and dive guides.

sections.heading: Elphinstone reef:
sections.text: A Red Sea legend. One of the most beautiful reefs, with its north and south plateau’s covered in hard and soft corals, and visiting pelagics, this truly is an awesome reef.

sections.heading: Zabargad:
sections.text: The island of Zabargad is an amazing dive spot. It is characterised by an enormous mountain reaching out of the water, surrounded by a lagoon and circling reef. There are a couple of wrecks and a great variety of corals and reef fish.

sections.heading: Rocky Island:
sections.text: Rocky Island hosts a fringing reef that circles the entire perimeter of the island, dropping steeply to astonishing depths, although the most interesting features and life are found above 12m. Watch the blue for life but take care as there can be strong currents. Cave reef is located one hour north of the main St. John’s area. Have fun finding your way through tunnels and around pinnacles. Beautiful dive site at the Red Sea.

sections.heading: St. John’s Reef:
sections.text: Located on the Tropic of Cancer, this chain of reefs is the furthest South you will get! All its dive sites are very close to each other which means that you can easily move from one place to another. It, therefore, adds a lot of variety to your dives: drop-offs, tunnels, and stunning hard-coral formations. One of these dives (St. John’s Caves or Umm Kharalim) is truly unique and is a photographer's heaven with rays of light filtering through into the beautiful tunnels.

sections.heading: St. John’s Reef North:
sections.text: Located one hour north of the main St. John’s area. Have fun finding your way through tunnels and around pinnacles. Marine Life: Wrecks, rays, Oceanic Whitetip sharks, octopus, lionfish, nudibranchs, frogfish, huge schools of fish, bright colourful reefs.

On this safari divers will have the opportunity to explore a variety of truly unique dive sites home to some very interesting and… Cave reef is located one hour north of the main St. John’s area. Have fun finding your way through tunnels and around pinnacles. A beautiful dive site at the Red Sea.

sections.heading: Fury Shoal:
sections.text: An immense chain of reefs creating a host of outstanding dive sites including Abu Galawa in the north to Sataya in the south. Have fun exploring caves, tunnels, coral gardens, plateaus, and drop-offs! Abu Galawa is located within Fury Shoal – have fun exploring the wreck of ‘Tug Boat’. The reef also has good coral dives on the west side.

sections.heading: Marine Life:
sections.text: Rays, sharks, octopus, lionfish, nudibranchs, frogfish, huge schools of fish, bright colorful reefs, Deep drop-offs covered with vibrant corals in the bluest of the blue sea. Shark and other large pelagic are common as they come into the reef and up from the deep. This is an astounding reef safari and a photographer’s dream. All dive sites are subject to weather conditions and the final route taken is at the absolute discretion of the captain and dive guides. Start and end in Port Ghalib; this tour visits reefs between Port Ghalib and St. Johns.

carlton::Classic North (Sharm El Sheikh.name: Classic North (Sharm El Sheikh - Sharm El Sheikh)
carlton::Classic North (Sharm El Sheikh.experience: Open Water - 30 minimum logged dives required.
carlton::Classic North (Sharm El Sheikh.intro: The Red Sea is a great place to dive year-round; the best time to go is from spring to fall, when the weather is mild and visibility is good. The Red Sea is home to a diverse and vibrant ecosystem, and it is a popular destination for divers from all over the world. The region is home to a variety of shipwrecks, from historic vessels to modern freighters. These wrecks provide a fascinating glimpse into the past, and they are also home to a wide variety of marine life. If you are interested in wreck diving, the Red Sea is a great place to go. Some of the best dive sites include Tiran Island and Ras Mohammed National Park, both offering excellent diving opportunities for beginners and experienced divers. You will dive multiple times a day during a weeklong liveaboard, typically three dives per day, with night dives also offered and plenty of time in between to relax, eat, and socialize. We customize your trip to fit your interests and experience level.

sections.heading: Day 1:
sections.text: Arrive at Sharm El Sheikh International Airport for a meet-and-greet service. Transfer to Travco Jetty – light dinner – safety briefing – cabin arrangement and equipment setup.

sections.heading: Day 2:
sections.text: The boat departs early in the morning at 07:00. After breakfast, you'll complete a check dive at the nearby dive site, Temple. The second dive is at Jackfish Alley in Ras Mohammed National Park. Sail to Beacon Rock for a dive at Coral Garden, followed by an optional night dive.

sections.heading: Day 3:
sections.text: Early morning dive at Shark and Yolanda Reef – sail to the SS Thistlegorm. Enjoy two dives at Shaab Ali, with the opportunity to swim with dolphins. Optional night dive.

sections.heading: Day 4:
sections.text: Early morning dive at Kingston Reef – second dive at Small Crack – third dive at the Dunraven Wreck – optional night dive at Beacon Rock.

sections.heading: Day 5:
sections.text: Early morning dives at Ras Zatar, Ras Ghozlani, and Ras Um Sid. Optional night dive.

sections.heading: Day 6:
sections.text: Tiran – early morning dive at Gordon Reef – second and third dives at Jackson Reef and Woodhouse Reef – optional night dive at Gordon Reef.

sections.heading: Day 7:
sections.text: Early morning dive at Thomas Reef – second dive at Ras Katy or Million Hope. Return to port at noon.

sections.heading: Day 8:
sections.text: Check out no later than 10:00.

sections.heading: Ocean Life:
sections.text: This route takes in some of the richest marine life in the northern Red Sea: reef sharks and Napoleon wrasse along the walls of Ras Mohammed, resident jackfish and glassfish at Jackfish Alley, batfish and turtles around the SS Thistlegorm wreck, dolphins at Shaab Ali, and strong currents at Tiran drawing in schools of snapper, jack, and eagle rays. The last dive will be on the penultimate day of the trip. Divers are recommended to wait for 24 hours before flying after the last dive.

destiny::Brothers - Daedalus - Elphinsto.name: Brothers - Daedalus - Elphinstone (Hurghada - Hurghada)
destiny::Brothers - Daedalus - Elphinsto.experience: Advanced Open Water - 50 minimum logged dives required.

sections.heading: Brother Islands
sections.text: The Brothers Islands are among the top five dive sites in the Red Sea. These islands, located about a kilometer apart, are actually pinnacles formed by volcanic activity. The larger island lies to the north, and the smaller one further south. These narrow, rocky pinnacles are surrounded only by the open sea and, due to their distance from the mainland, are only accessible by liveaboard dive boat. Rising from great depths, they are known as drop-off dive sites. The steep walls are densely covered with hard and soft corals. Their location can result in strong currents, which contribute to a large shark population and have made the Brothers famous. Sightings of grey reef sharks, oceanic whitetip sharks (Longimanus), thresher sharks, hammerhead sharks, and silky sharks are not uncommon.

sections.heading: Big Brother
sections.text: Even from afar, you can see the landmark of the dive site – the lighthouse built in 1883. At the northern tip of the island, the Numidia sank in 1901. A 145-meter-long English merchant ship carrying railway parts, the wreck lies upright at a depth of between 8 and 85 meters on the sloping reef. The cargo hold and gallery are open and accessible to divers. 46 years later, another merchant ship sank on the west side – the Aida II. Due to a sudden change in weather, the ship sought shelter near the islands and struck the reef upon landing, immediately taking on water. Today, the Aida lies at a depth of 25 to 60 meters. After all these years, nature has reclaimed the wrecks. The hulls and superstructures are beautifully covered with gorgonians, sponges, and soft corals. On the southern plateau, there is a shark cleaning station. With a bit of luck, thresher sharks and manta rays gather here.

sections.heading: Little brother
sections.text: The sheer edge of the west face looks almost unreal. Full of color and life. The entire drop-off is vibrant and teeming with marine life. Vast sea fan colonies lead to dense forests of vibrantly colored soft corals. Monumental stony coral formations on the east wall provide refuge for a multitude of reef fish. Longnose hawk fish make their home among the gorgonians. Groupers, pufferfish, tropical triggerfish, boxfish, clownfish, and stingrays, as well as pulsating clouds of fiery anthias, can all be found there. If you manage to momentarily ignore the wild chaos of the reef fish and gaze out into the blue, you might just encounter a surprise: snapper, mackerel, barracuda, tuna, Napoleon wrasse, and turtles are not uncommon. So boredom is certainly not an option.

sections.heading: Daedalus
sections.text: When the lighthouse on Abu Kizan (its Arabic name) was built in 1863, no one could have imagined what lay beneath the surface of this hotspot. The reef gained its fame due to its large population of hammerhead sharks. The good news: both groups are resident and therefore always present at the reef. The bad news: they aren't always visible, as they patrol depths inaccessible to recreational divers. Daedalus is the reef of unlimited possibilities – anything that's anyone in the Red Sea can pass by. Sightings of thresher sharks are no longer uncommon. Along with the Brothers Islands and a few dive sites in the Philippines, Daedalus is a guarantee for seeing these beauties with their distinctive tail fins. The gentle giants also love this spot. Several manta ray sightings and encounters with whale sharks help secure this spot as a top-class position worldwide. The dive site, however, demands a certain level of diving skill. Strong, constantly changing currents are the norm and precisely why they are so popular with marine life. Knowing how to deploy a surface marker buoy is absolutely essential here. The descent into the open water without seeing a reef can also cause some divers a queasy feeling in their stomach. This is quickly forgotten, however, when the first scalloped hammerhead shark is spotted and the diver has to clear their mask for the first time because water has entered due to its big grin. Things are more relaxed on the southern plateau. From 20 meters down, A gently sloping plateau dotted with numerous ergs. Groupers, moray eels, and Napoleon wrasse abound on the plateau. Turtles also frequent the many soft corals. Depending on the season, oceanic whitetip sharks and silky sharks gather beneath the safari boats.

sections.heading: Elphinstone (Arabic: "Abu Hamra")
sections.text: Arguably the most famous dive site in all of Egypt, Elphinstone owes its name, "Red Rock," to a red rock formation on the mainland that sailors once used as a navigational aid. The approximately 600-meter-long, spindle-shaped reef lies just 9 kilometers off the Egyptian coast and is a popular spot for daily dives offered by various dive centers and a highlight at the end of any dive safari. Despite the high volume of diving activity, the underwater inhabitants are undeterred. Elphinstone is renowned for its high concentration of oceanic whitetip sharks (also known as longimanus). Nowhere else on the planet is the probability of encountering one of the largest shark species so high. Some females can reach a size of up to 3 meters. Elphinstone is a drop-off reef with a northern and southern plateau. The steep walls plunge hundreds of meters into the deep blue – an eerie yet beautiful contrast to the reef's many colorful coral species, especially the purple and pink soft corals and graceful red gorgonians – their tentacles swaying in the strong currents. Depending on the prevailing current (usually from north to south), the dive begins at the northern plateau. Experienced divers start very deep at the level of the erg to increase their chances of spotting hammerhead sharks. They then drift southwards at a reduced depth. The dive ends in open water with a deployed surface marker buoy, waiting for the oceanic whitetip sharks and completing the safety stop, which can be extended if the first rounded dorsal fin is spotted and there's still enough air in the tank. However, one should keep an eye out for the blue water throughout the dive. Bottlenose dolphins, manta rays, marlin, whale sharks, and other shark species can pass by at any time. Halfway to the southern plateau, you'll usually encounter a huge, resident Napoleon wreck. He's not shy around divers and often looks them straight in the eye or gives them a friendly nudge. For technical divers, the sarcophagus, also known as the archway, is interesting and accessible. Legend has it that an Egyptian pharaoh is buried here. Even in low light, the shape of a sarcophagus is recognizable, and it's covered in coral. The archway begins at approximately 52 meters and ends at 62 meters; you'll need the correct air mixture in your tank to reach it. Also on the northern plateau...Technical divers have a good chance of encountering hammerhead sharks. The breach at the northern plateau is no less spectacular. Shortly before the erg, at about 50 meters, you'll find three large sea fans marking the entrance to the breach. From there, the dive continues at a depth of approximately 48 to 53 meters, traversing the entire northern plateau. This lies well below the depth limit for recreational divers and should only be attempted with the necessary technical training and the correct air mixture.

sections.text: is a popular Red Sea diving area offering a mix of stunning coral gardens, lagoons, and playful dolphin encounters. The site features impressive hard coral structures, diverse marine life, and calm conditions ideal for relaxed, scenic dives. Its beautiful underwater landscapes make it a favorite for both beginners and experienced divers.

sections.heading: St. Johns
sections.text: is a remote and pristine reef system in the southern Red Sea, known for its dramatic coral formations, maze-like swim-throughs, and excellent visibility. Divers can expect vibrant soft corals, abundant reef fish, and frequent encounters with turtles, rays, and the occasional shark. Its isolated location offers peaceful, uncrowded dives perfect for all experience levels.

destiny::Fury Shoals - Elphinstone - Saf.experience: Advanced Open Water - 50 minimum logged dives required.
destiny::Fury Shoals - Elphinstone - Saf.intro: Fury Shoals is a popular Red Sea diving area offering a mix of stunning coral gardens, lagoons, and playful dolphin encounters. The site features impressive hard coral structures, diverse marine life, and calm conditions ideal for relaxed, scenic dives. Its beautiful underwater landscapes make it a favorite for both beginners and experienced divers. Elphinstone (Arabic: "Abu Hamra"). Arguably the most famous dive site in all of Egypt, Elphinstone owes its name, "Red Rock," to a red rock formation on the mainland that sailors once used as a navigational aid. The approximately 600-meter-long, spindle-shaped reef lies just 9 kilometers off the Egyptian coast and is a popular spot for daily dives offered by various dive centers and a highlight at the end of any dive safari. Despite the high volume of diving activity, the underwater inhabitants are undeterred. Elphinstone is renowned for its high concentration of oceanic whitetip sharks (also known as longimanus). Nowhere else on the planet is the probability of encountering one of the largest shark species so high. Some females can reach a size of up to 3 meters. Elphinstone is a drop-off reef with a northern and southern plateau. The steep walls plunge hundreds of meters into the deep blue — an eerie yet beautiful contrast to the reef's many colorful coral species, especially the purple and pink soft corals and graceful red gorgonians, their tentacles swaying in the strong currents. Depending on the prevailing current (usually from north to south), the dive begins at the northern plateau. Experienced divers start very deep at the level of the erg to increase their chances of spotting hammerhead sharks. They then drift southwards at a reduced depth. The dive ends in open water with a deployed surface marker buoy, waiting for the oceanic whitetip sharks and completing the safety stop, which can be extended if the first rounded dorsal fin is spotted and there's still enough air in the tank. However, one should keep an eye out for the blue water throughout the dive. Bottlenose dolphins, manta rays, marlin, whale sharks, and other shark species can pass by at any time. Halfway to the southern plateau, you'll usually encounter a huge, resident Napoleon wrasse. He's not shy around divers and often looks them straight in the eye or gives them a friendly nudge. For technical divers, the sarcophagus, also known as the archway, is interesting and accessible. Legend has it that an Egyptian pharaoh is buried here. Even in low light, the shape of a sarcophagus is recognizable, and it's covered in coral. The archway begins at approximately 52 meters and ends at 62 meters; you'll need the correct air mixture in your tank to reach it. Also on the northern plateau, technical divers have a good chance of encountering hammerhead sharks. The breach at the northern plateau is no less spectacular. Shortly before the erg, at about 50 meters, you'll find three large sea fans marking the entrance to the breach. From there, the dive continues at a depth of approximately 48 to 53 meters, traversing the entire northern plateau. This lies well below the depth limit for recreational divers and should only be attempted with the necessary technical training and the correct air mixture. Best of Safaga: Panorama Reef (Arabic: "Abu Alama"). "Father of the Mast," a concrete pillar that once marked the northern end, has now been replaced by a state-of-the-art automatic beacon. The 400-meter-deep drop-offs and strong currents are facts that worry many a diver at Panorama Reef. However, the mere mention of "big fish" is enough to see some diving enthusiasts already in their wetsuits. The deep blue waters and the vibrant colors of the corals create a stunning contrast. In summer, whale shark and manta ray sightings are not uncommon. Eagle rays, Napoleon wrasse, and large turtles have also established themselves here and happily pose for the camera. On the southern plateau, which drops to a depth of 35 meters, you'll find enormous gorgonians growing on a chimney. Hundreds of clownfish frolic in a vast field of anemones.

sections.heading: North of Hurghada
sections.text: , the Red Sea resembles a shipwreck graveyard. Here, the sea splits into two arms of the Gulf, Aqaba and Suez. The Suez Canal remains one of the busiest trade routes. Numerous offshore islands and reefs have caused many ships to perish, creating a wreck paradise for divers today.

sections.heading: The Brothers Islands
sections.text: are among the top five dive sites in the Red Sea. These two islands are about a kilometer apart and are actually mountain peaks formed by volcanic activity. The larger of the two lies to the north, and the smaller of the two, Little Brother, further south. These narrow, rocky pinnacles are surrounded by nothing but the open sea and, due to their distance from the mainland, are only accessible by liveaboard boat. Rising from great depths, they are known as drop-offs. The steep walls are densely covered with hard and soft corals. Their location can lead to strong currents, which contribute to the high shark populations and have made the Brothers famous. Sightings of grey reef sharks, oceanic whitetip sharks, thresher sharks, hammerhead sharks, and silky sharks are not uncommon.

sections.heading: Big Brother
sections.text: Even from a distance, you can see the landmark of the dive site – the lighthouse built in 1883. At the northern tip of the island, the Numidia sank in 1901. A 145-meter-long English merchant ship carrying railway parts, the wreck lies upright at a depth of between 8 and 85 meters on the sloping reef. The cargo hold and gallery are open and accessible to divers. 46 years later, another merchant ship sank on the west side – the Aida II. Due to a sudden change in the weather, the ship sought shelter near the islands, struck the sea while docking, and immediately began to fill with water. Today, the Aida lies at a depth of 25 to 60 meters. After all these years, nature has reclaimed the wrecks. The hulls and superstructures are beautifully covered with gorgonians, sponges, and soft corals. On the southern plateau, there is a shark cleaning station. With a bit of luck, thresher sharks and manta rays gather here.

sections.heading: Little brother
sections.text: The " Little Brother " The sheer drop-off of the west wall seems almost unreal. Full of color and life. The entire drop-off is vibrant and teeming with marine life – enormous sea fan colonies lead to dense forests of colorful soft corals. Monumental stony coral formations on the east wall offer refuge to a multitude of reef fish. Longnose hawkfish find their home among the gorgonians. Groupers, pufferfish, tropical triggerfish, boxfish, clownfish, and stingrays, as well as pulsating clouds of fiery anthias, abound. If you manage to ignore the wild chaos of the reef fish for a moment and gaze out into the blue, you might just be in for a surprise: snapper, mackerel, barracuda, tuna, Napoleon wrasse, and turtles are not uncommon here. You certainly won't get bored.

sections.heading: SS Thistlegorm
sections.text: The British freighter was bombed on October 6, 1941, during World War II, was hit in the stern and sunk. Despite effective defenses such as machine guns and anti-aircraft guns, nine crew members were unable to return to their safe harbor. The remaining crew were captured by unknown persons and taken prisoner in Australia. In 1956, Jacques-Yves Cousteau set out to locate the wreck. The expedition team recovered some parts, including the captain's safe. However, this contained only decayed ship's papers. Cousteau never revealed the wreck's location, and so in 1991, German recreational divers resumed the search. The well-preserved wreck, its construction, and its cargo make it one of the most popular dive sites in the Red Sea today. Motorcycles, trucks, and even a railway wagon lie at a depth of approximately 30 meters. The steam locomotive's engine, which was thrown away by the enormous force of the explosion, also lies nearby. The bridge rises 17 meters high. A beautiful little biotope teeming with reef fish has developed over the years. The dive is suitable for all experience levels, but the current should not be underestimated. At 126 meters in length, penetration into the interior of the wreck is possible, but for safety reasons, the dive guide's instructions must be followed precisely. Given the ongoing corrosion, it is expected that the heavily stressed deck sections will eventually collapse. The remaining portion of ammunition and explosives is also decomposing. In 2007, HEPCA installed a system of anchor lines to ensure the preservation of this beautiful dive site for many years to come.

sections.heading: Abu Nuhas
sections.text: Abu Nuhas is a legendary reef in the northern Red Sea off the coast of Egypt, infamous among sailors and beloved by divers. The shallow, elongated reef lies near the Strait of Gubal – a busy shipping lane – and has claimed the lives of numerous cargo ships over the decades. Strong currents, navigational errors, and poor visibility have led to many vessels running aground and sinking. Today, at least five easily accessible wrecks rest close together on its northern side: the Carnatic, Giannis D, Chrisoula K, and Kimon M. Every dive at Abu Nuhas is a journey into history – with impressive wreck structures, fascinating cargo, and an abundance of marine life. An absolute highlight for wreck divers. Another very worthwhile wreck to see is the..

sections.heading: Rosalie Moller
sections.text: The British coal freighter Rosalie Moller was built in 1910 and served as a supply ship during the Second World War. On October 8, 1941, she was sunk by German bombers, just two days after the famous Thistlegorm, which lies further south. The Rosalie Moller was at anchor when she was attacked by a German Heinkel He 111. She sank during the night to a depth of about 50 meters and remained virtually undiscovered for decades. The Rosalie Moller lies upright at a depth of approximately 50 meters, with the deck beginning at around 30 to 35 meters. The hull is still largely intact and impresses with its size, stability, and depth. The superstructure, winches, and cargo areas are well preserved – the original character of a coal transporter is clearly recognizable. The masts still stand, but are covered in coral and sponges. Due to the greater depth, visibility is often limited (10–20 meters), and the light is more subdued, giving the dive a mystical atmosphere. The bombs hit the Rosalie Moller on the starboard side and are still clearly visible today. The wreck now lies in a military restricted area, so diving is only possible on rare occasions. Its distinguishing feature is the large "M" on the funnel.

sections.heading: Abu Kafan
sections.text: Translated from Arabic as "Father of the Deep," this name for the approximately 300-meter-long reef was undoubtedly well-deserved. It plunges to depths of up to 700 meters into the deep blue! While not always easy to navigate due to the potential for strong currents, this dive site is considered one of the best in all of Safaga. Two beautiful plateaus form the base and base of the steep walls. The southern side is usually sheltered and often used as an anchorage for boats. Just below the surface, sloping down to about 18 meters, lies a stunning, column-like formation that immediately captures the attention of divers. With good air consumption, it's worthwhile to circumnavigate this column several times at different depths, as it teems with marine life. A trained eye will spot the well-camouflaged stonefish, scorpionfish, and even crocodilefish among the corals. The northern plateau is no less spectacular—quite the opposite. In good weather and calm seas, the north side can be dived. Extending to a depth of approximately 22-28 meters, it plunges vertically into the open sea. Here, two large coral blocks stand, covered in fantastic coral growth. Large fish of all kinds can be spotted here. Reef sharks, a school of resident barracuda, as well as turtles, Napoleon wrasse, and manta rays are among the local heroes. The almost vertical east wall is adorned with beautiful soft corals, gorgonians, and black coral, practically begging to be explored on a drift dive. About halfway down, at a depth of 17 meters, a deep crevice juts into the wall, and shortly after, it continues as a canyon. The entire east wall is riddled with numerous small caves, crevices, and impressive overhangs, providing a fantastic habitat for a wide variety of marine life. As beautiful as this wall is to behold, please never forget to check the open water below! The west side is not as spectacularly overgrown, but it is also good enough for a nice drift dive.

destiny::North Tiran - Dahab (Hurghada -.intro: This itinerary explores the northern Red Sea’s most iconic reefs and wrecks, combining the vibrant dive sites of the Tiran Straits with the dramatic landscapes of Dahab. The route features colorful coral gardens, steep walls, and world-famous sites such as Ras Mohammed and the Blue Hole area, offering a varied mix of reef, wall, and drift diving. With generally milder currents, excellent visibility, and diverse marine life, this journey is ideal for divers seeking classic Red Sea scenery, rich biodiversity, and relaxed yet rewarding diving.

sections.heading: The Brother Islands
sections.text: (El Akhawein) are the pinnacles of two undersea mountains rising from the depths of the abyss, 300 m deep, and are located about 60 miles offshore. Big Brother, which is easily identified with its lighthouse, is about 100 meters across and 400 meters in length, with two extremities to the east and west. Little Brother lies about 800 meters east of Big Brother. As part of the Marine Park Islands National Park, these islands offer stunning wall diving and a breathtaking display of color with their wide variety of soft corals and gorgonians, which cover the walls. You will find large and small fish here in abundance; tuna, barracuda, shoals of snappers and jackfish, as well as hammerheads, silky and oceanic whitetip sharks, even the occasional thresher shark and manta ray. Sightings of the Grey Reef Shark are almost guaranteed on the North and South Plateaux of Small Brother. For the wreck diver, the wrecks of the Aida II, an 82 m long Egyptian supply vessel that sank in 1957, and the Numidia, a cargo ship carrying locomotive spare parts to India, lie on the walls of the Big Brother. Both are covered in a rich growth of soft and hard corals. Marine life includes a family of Napoleon Wrasse and Grey Reef Sharks.

sections.heading: Daedalus Reef
sections.text: , also part of the Marine Park, is a large, oval reef with a lighthouse and is the furthest offshore reef in the Egyptian Red Sea. Its deep walls and drop-offs offer some of the most spectacular diving to be found. Daedalus has mountainous, pristine, hard coral formations. There is also a strong chance of spotting schooling Hammerheads, and grey reef sharks.

sections.heading: Elphinstone,
sections.text: with its sheer walls covered in soft corals, offers a likely encounter with Grey Reef Sharks circling on the plateaux, and even Oceanic White Tip Sharks can be seen here for most of the year.

Big Brother, which is easily identified with its lighthouse, is about 100 metres across and 400 metres in length, with two extremities to the east and west. You will find large and small fish here in abundance; tuna, barracuda, shoals of snappers and jackfish, as well as hammerheads, silky and oceanic whitetip sharks, even the occasional thresher shark and manta ray. Sightings of the Grey Reef Shark are almost guaranteed on the North and South Plateaux of Small Brother. For the wreck diver, the wrecks of the Aida II, an 82 m long Egyptian supply vessel that sank in 1957, and the Numidia, a cargo ship carrying locomotive spare parts to India, lie on the walls of the Big Brother. discovery-i::North Wrecks, Ras Mohamed,.name: 15% Off: North Wrecks, Ras Mohamed, Tiran (Hurghada - Hurghada)
discovery-i::North Wrecks, Ras Mohamed,.experience: Open Water - 10 minimum logged dives required.
discovery-i::North Wrecks, Ras Mohamed,.intro: This Red Sea diving safari offers a mixed itinerary of wreck diving and reef diving. You will visit the most impressive wrecks in the Northern Red Sea, as well as stunning reef diving. This cruise has something for everyone. Starting from Hurghada and sailing north gives a perfect combination of reef diving and wreck diving. The famous horseshoe-shaped reef of Shaab El Erg is a perfect example of the reefs on offer on this cruise, with its beautiful hard coral garden and the chance to see dolphins. Abu Nuhas has four well-known wrecks: Giannis D, Carnatic, the lentil wreck and the tile wreck, all offering spectacular dives and plenty of fish life. Night dives can be superb in this area. Gubal Island offers protected anchoring for the night. A small wreck at 8-10 metres makes for a spectacular night dive with lionfish, scorpion fish and its resident giant moray eel.

sections.heading: Dunraven
sections.text: The wreck of this 72m-long English steamer lies at the southern point of Shaab Mahmoud, amongst the series of shallow reefs and lagoons. Sunk in 1876 on its way from Bombay to England carrying a cargo of spices and timber, her hull lies upside down at a maximum depth of 29m. Completely covered in corals, the wreck has become home to a wide variety of marine life including glass fish, morays, groupers, goatfish and napoleon.

sections.heading: Sha’ab Abu Nuhas
sections.text: This great reef, also known as the “ships graveyard”, emerges two miles to the north of Shedwan Island at the mouth of the Strait of Gobal. On the seabed of the surrounding area lie no fewer than seven sunken ships from different eras. It is often only possible to dive the wrecks from a zodiac due to the heavy sea swells. On the sheltered south side of the reef are two beautiful ergs known as the Yellow Fish Reef. These make an excellent night dive.

sections.heading: Giannis D
sections.text: This large Greek freighter hit the reef in1983 and slowly sank over six weeks. The wreck is split into two sections, lying at a maximum depth of 28 metres. The stern section is the most impressive because it can be entered through the many entries and exit points, although it can be disorientating due to the angle at which the wreck lies. The engine room is full of glass fish, and it is possible to observe all sorts of fish swimming by, including snappers, jacks, eagle rays and sharks.

sections.heading: Carnatic
sections.text: The Carnatic was a splendid 90-metre-long sail and engine steamer launched by P&O in 1862. Carrying a cargo of wine and “London soda water” in distinctive oval bottles, it was sailing the Indies route with a destination of Bombay. It struck the reef in 1869 and remained aground for a number of hours before sinking. She lies on one side with the stern at 24 metres and the bow at 16 metres. The decking of the hull has fallen away, exposing blackened support structures which are now draped in hard and soft corals. The very photogenic wreck is now home to a number of morays, large grouper and octopuses.

sections.heading: Jackson Reef
sections.text: Most northerly of the reefs of Tiran and the northern limit of day boats from Sharm El Sheikh. The wreck of the “Lara” lies at the northern end. There is superb wall diving along its entire perimeter, with numerous buttresses and gullies. Sightings of sharks, turtles and other big fish are not uncommon, and you will find a huge diversity of different corals and sponges as well as clouds of triggerfish, masked puffers and bannerfish. At this point, you may be lucky and spot a Hammerhead in summer.

sections.heading: Thomas Reef
sections.text: Between Gordon and Woodhouse reefs, a smaller round reef with walls plunging deep and fully covered with soft coral, gorgonians and colourful fish life. It is almost possible to circumnavigate this reef in one dive. The east wall plunges dramatically to great depths with a mass of brightly coloured soft corals. The west wall is darker with overhangs and caves but is a great drift dive with sightings of Trevally and Tuna in the blue and schooling reef fish close to the reef.

sections.heading: Ras Mohammed
sections.text: Really, several dive sites, Ras Mohammed has earned itself a reputation as one of the top dive sites in the world, here at the tip of the Sinai, where the vast bodies of water, the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba meet, have created an ecosystem like no other and wall diving at its very best.

sections.heading: The SS Thistlegorm
sections.text: A short ride across the Straits of Gubal and you visit the most famous wreck of the Red Sea, the SS Thistlegorm! An awe-inspiring World War II British vessel with a cargo full of armaments (Bedford trucks and BSA motorbikes), which were all destined for the British troops in North Africa. She was sunk by the German Luftwaffe and now lies in 30 metres of water. Depending on divers’ experience, weather and current conditions, we also try to offer a night dive here.

sections.heading: The Brother Islands
sections.text: The Brother Islands are the pinnacles of two undersea mountains rising from the depths of the abyss and are located about 60 miles offshore from El Quesir. Part of the Marine Park Islands National Park, these islands offer stunning wall diving, with the walls being covered in soft corals and forests of gorgonians, creating a kaleidoscope of ever-changing colours. They attract a diverse array of marine species and large pelagics. Large tuna, Barracudas, Jacks and Snappers cruise in the blue, accompanied by occasional Hammerheads, Silky and oceanic white-tip sharks and Mantas. Both are covered in a rich growth of soft and hard corals. Marine life includes a family of Napoleon Wrasse and Grey Reef Sharks. The boat will then sail back to Hurghada via Safaga, where you can dive at Panorama Reef or the famous wreck of Salem Express for a memorable finale!

discovery-i::St. John's, Fury Shoal, Elp.experience: Open Water - 10 minimum logged dives required.
discovery-i::St. John's, Fury Shoal, Elp.intro: Sailing to the southernmost reefs, these cruises depart from Marsa Ghalib to the vast reef system of Fury Shoals and St John’s. At Fury Shoals, dive Shaab Claude with its famous swim-throughs and huge porite corals. White Tip Reef sharks and an anemone and clownfish settlement can be seen a little off the reef to the South. Abu Galawa Soraya has a fantastic coral garden and a wreck of a private sailing boat packed with glass fish. Dive Shab Sharm, with its wall dives and White Tip Reef sharks. Oceanic White Tips and Silky sharks can sometimes be found in the blue, and turtles often visit the South side before heading further south to Wadi Gamal, with its flowing banks of hard yellow and green soft coral, resident angel and butterfly fish, and in the right season huge schools of placid jack and tuna visit the area. St John’s is a vast collection of small reefs offering some of the most remote and rewarding diving in the Red Sea. Habili Ali offers giant gorgonians and black corals whilst Grey Reef, Silvertip, and schools of Hammerhead sharks might be found on the west side. Habili Gafaar is a mass of soft corals teaming with shoals of snappers, butterfly fish, and barracudas. Mantas, Grey Reef, and Silvertip sharks can be seen in the blue. Gota Kebir is a massive reef, famous for its tunnels and south plateau, where jacks and barracudas can be seen, as well as the occasional manta. The tunnels are ideal for novice cave divers. Gota Soraya is rated as possibly one of the best wall dives in the Red Sea, with overhangs and cracks in the reef wall full of glass fish and sweepers and an abundance of corals, Grey Reef, Silvertips, and Hammerhead sharks. Elphinstone, with its sheer walls covered in soft corals, offers a likely encounter with Grey Reef Sharks circling on the plateaux, and even Oceanic White Tip Sharks can be seen here for most of the year.

discovery-ii::North Wrecks, Ras Mohamed,.intro: This Red Sea diving safari offers a mixed itinerary of wreck diving and reef diving. You will visit the most impressive wrecks in the Northern Red Sea, as well as stunning reef diving. This cruise has something for everyone. Starting from Hurghada and sailing north gives a perfect combination of reef diving and wreck diving. The famous horseshoe-shaped reef of Shaab El Erg is a perfect example of the reefs on offer on this cruise, with its beautiful hard coral garden and the chance to see dolphins. Abu Nuhas has four well-known wrecks: Giannis D, Carnatic, the lentil wreck and the tile wreck, all offering spectacular dives and plenty of fish life. Night dives can be superb in this area. Gubal Island offers protected anchoring for the night. A small wreck at 8-10 metres makes for a spectacular night dive with lionfish, scorpion fish and its resident giant moray eel.

sections.heading: Dunraven
sections.text: The wreck of this 72m-long English steamer lies at the southern point of Shaab Mahmoud, amongst the series of shallow reefs and lagoons. Sunk in 1876 on its way from Bombay to England carrying a cargo of spices and timber, her hull lies upside down at a maximum depth of 29m. Completely covered in corals, the wreck has become home to a wide variety of marine life including glass fish, morays, groupers, goatfish and napoleon.

sections.heading: Sha’ab Abu Nuhas
sections.text: This great reef, also known as the “ships graveyard”, emerges two miles to the north of Shedwan Island at the mouth of the Strait of Gobal. On the seabed of the surrounding area lie no fewer than seven sunken ships from different eras. It is often only possible to dive the wrecks from a zodiac due to the heavy sea swells. On the sheltered south side of the reef are two beautiful ergs known as the Yellow Fish Reef. These make an excellent night dive.

sections.heading: Giannis D
sections.text: This large Greek freighter hit the reef in1983 and slowly sank over six weeks. The wreck is split into two sections, lying at a maximum depth of 28 metres. The stern section is the most impressive because it can be entered through the many entries and exit points, although it can be disorientating due to the angle at which the wreck lies. The engine room is full of glass fish, and it is possible to observe all sorts of fish swimming by, including snappers, jacks, eagle rays and sharks.

sections.heading: Carnatic
sections.text: The Carnatic was a splendid 90-metre-long sail and engine steamer launched by P&O in 1862. Carrying a cargo of wine and “London soda water” in distinctive oval bottles, it was sailing the Indies route with a destination of Bombay. It struck the reef in 1869 and remained aground for a number of hours before sinking. She lies on one side with the stern at 24 metres and the bow at 16 metres. The decking of the hull has fallen away, exposing blackened support structures which are now draped in hard and soft corals. The very photogenic wreck is now home to a number of morays, large grouper and octopuses.

sections.heading: Jackson Reef
sections.text: Most northerly of the reefs of Tiran and the northern limit of day boats from Sharm El Sheikh. The wreck of the “Lara” lies at the northern end. There is superb wall diving along its entire perimeter, with numerous buttresses and gullies. Sightings of sharks, turtles and other big fish are not uncommon, and you will find a huge diversity of different corals and sponges as well as clouds of triggerfish, masked puffers and bannerfish. At this point, you may be lucky and spot a Hammerhead in summer.

sections.heading: Thomas Reef
sections.text: Between Gordon and Woodhouse reefs, a smaller round reef with walls plunging deep and fully covered with soft coral, gorgonians and colourful fish life. It is almost possible to circumnavigate this reef in one dive. The east wall plunges dramatically to great depths with a mass of brightly coloured soft corals. The west wall is darker with overhangs and caves but is a great drift dive with sightings of Trevally and Tuna in the blue and schooling reef fish close to the reef.

sections.heading: Ras Mohammed
sections.text: Really, several dive sites, Ras Mohammed has earned itself a reputation as one of the top dive sites in the world, here at the tip of the Sinai, where the vast bodies of water, the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba meet, have created an ecosystem like no other and wall diving at its very best.

sections.heading: The SS Thistlegorm
sections.text: A short ride across the Straits of Gubal and you visit the most famous wreck of the Red Sea, the SS Thistlegorm! An awe-inspiring World War II British vessel with a cargo full of armaments (Bedford trucks and BSA motorbikes), which were all destined for the British troops in North Africa. She was sunk by the German Luftwaffe and now lies in 30 metres of water. Depending on divers’ experience, weather and current conditions, we also try to offer a night dive here.

sections.text: is a beautiful reef system which lies approx. 40km north of the Sudanese border and 20 km south of Zabargad. Abu Galawa Soraya has a fantastic coral garden and a wreck of a private sailing boat packed with glass fish. Dive Shab Sharm, with its wall dives and White Tip Reef sharks. Oceanic White Tips and Silky sharks can sometimes be found in the blue, and turtles often visit the South side before heading further south to Wadi Gamal, with its flowing banks of hard yellow and green soft coral, resident angel and butterfly fish, and in the right season huge schools of placid jack and tuna visit the area. St John’s is a vast collection of small reefs offering some of the most remote and rewarding diving in the Red Sea. Habili Ali offers giant gorgonians and black corals whilst Grey Reef, Silvertip, and schools of Hammerhead sharks might be found on the west side. sections.heading: Best of Egypt: A Premier Diving Adventure in Egypt
sections.text: Embark on an unforgettable journey with the Dune Liveaboard for a 15-day cruise from the North to the South of the Red Sea! Explore the underwater treasures of Ras Mohammed National Park, the Tiran Islands, and Dahab's famous Blue Hole. Then dive into history by exploring the SS Thistlegorm, a legendary wreck from the Second World War. Then head south for exciting dives around the offshore islands of Big Brother, Small Brother, and Daedalus, famous for their breathtaking walls covered in soft corals, gorgonians, and anemones, as well as encounters with longimanus, hammerhead, and grey reef sharks. Divers can also explore the wrecks of the Aida and Numidia, now covered in marine life. Continue on the spectacular landscapes of Rocky Island and Zabargad Island, both surrounded by reefs covered in colourful coral, where you can spot reef sharks, moray eels, and schools of barracuda. Zabargad, with its turquoise lagoons and unique coral formations, also offers a fascinating underwater labyrinth to explore. Finally, dive into the wonders of Saint John’s and Fury Shoals, a vast network of reefs offering an extraordinary diversity of marine life, from colourful coral gardens to caves and tunnels. Whether you're drifting through the pinnacles of Umm Arouk or drifting along the walls of Gotta Kebir, Saint John’s and Fury Shoals promise a captivating underwater adventure that will leave every diver begging for more.

sections.heading: Day 1: Arrival
sections.text: Our team will welcome you at the airport. You will be transferred by bus to the marina. Your cabin will then be assigned, and you will have the opportunity to explore the boat. Check in at 3 PM.

sections.heading: Day 2: Departure from Safaga/Hurghada
sections.text: After breakfast, a welcome briefing will be presented by the guide, covering the week's itinerary, onboard safety instructions, etc. Your diving documents and insurance will be checked before leaving the marina. The captain will head to the first diving site, just 30 minutes from departure, where the briefing for the "refresher" dive will take place. After lunch, you will perform the second dive of the day in the Hurghada area before continuing your journey northward to reach El Gouna, where you will spend the night at a site sheltered from the waves.

sections.heading: Day 3: Tiran
sections.text: On the third day of your trip, you'll have the chance to explore the island of Tiran. Located near the tip of Sinai, this island offers unique diving at several different sites. For your first dive, you'll discover the majestic and breathtaking Thomas Canyon. You'll then dive the northernmost site, Jackson Reef, where you may be lucky enough to spot sharks. Finally, Gordon Reef offers a lovely coral garden to end the day!

sections.heading: Day 4: Dahab and Nabq
sections.text: Explore the wonders of Dahab and Nabq, two iconic diving spots in Sinai. In Dahab, dive the Blue Hole and Canyon, known for dramatic drop-offs and vibrant marine life. Nabq offers tranquil waters, coral plateaus, and mangroves, with turtles and rays for all-level divers.

sections.heading: Day 5: Ras Mohamed and the Thistlegorm
sections.text: Discover the best of Ras Mohamed and the Thistlegorm, two iconic Red Sea dive sites. Ras Mohamed offers vibrant coral reefs, dramatic walls, and abundant marine life, making it a must-see for divers. At the Thistlegorm, explore the legendary WWII shipwreck, filled with fascinating artifacts and surrounded by schools of fish, creating a perfect mix of history and underwater adventure.

sections.heading: Day 6: Thistlegorm and Gubal
sections.text: Today, you will dive at least twice on the wreck of the SS Thistlegorm. Then, you will sail for two hours across the Strait of Gubal to reach the small island of Gubal, where you will make the third dive of the day.

sections.heading: Day 7: Abu Nuhas and Hurghada
sections.text: Explore Abu Nuhas and Hurghada, two gems of the Red Sea. Abu Nuhas is home to historic shipwrecks teeming with marine life, while Hurghada boasts vibrant reefs and an abundance of fish, perfect for divers of all levels.

sections.heading: Day 8: Safaga
sections.text: Explore the underwater wonders of Safaga, a prime diving destination in the Red Sea. Known for its vibrant coral reefs, diverse marine life, and clear waters, Safaga offers incredible dive sites like Panorama Reef and Abu Kafan, where you can experience breathtaking drop-offs, colorful gardens, and encounters with pelagic species. Perfect for divers of all levels, Safaga promises unforgettable underwater adventures.

sections.heading: Day 9: Brothers
sections.text: On the ninth day, you’ll dive at the iconic Brother Islands, starting with Big Brother’s dramatic coral walls and possible shark sightings. Next, explore Little Brother’s vibrant marine life and stunning soft corals. A third dive will wrap up this incredible day.

sections.heading: Day 10: Daedalus
sections.text: Three dives are offered at the Daedalus site, a potential meeting place with hammerhead sharks. A visit to the lighthouse may be organized by your guide, depending on agreements with the local keepers.

sections.heading: Day 11: Rocky Zabargad
sections.text: You will perform three dives around the Rocky and Zabargad islands. The navigation time between sites varies from 30 to 45 minutes. Dive sites are carefully selected by your guide based on the weather and the number of boats at each site.

sections.heading: Day 12: St. John’s
sections.text: Early in the morning, the captain and his crew will take you to the dive sites at St. John's. Three dives are planned for the day. The navigation times between sites in the St. John's area vary between 30 minutes and 1 hour and 30 minutes. Dive sites are carefully chosen by your guide based on the weather conditions and the number of boats present.

sections.heading: Day 13: Fury Shoals & Sheleneyat
sections.text: Today, we begin our journey northward. En route, we will stop at Sataya (Dolphin House) located in the Fury Shoals area, where you may have the opportunity to swim with dolphins. We will then continue north to the Sheleneyat site in the Wadi Gemal area, where the third dive of the day will take place at twilight or night.

sections.heading: Day 14: Elphinstone Reef
sections.text: In the early morning, you will arrive in the Marsa Alam area at the legendary Elphinstone Reef. You will conduct two dives there, before sailing for another two hours to reach Port Ghalib Marina in the early afternoon. You can use the rear platform to rinse your gear. Your guide will also offer various non-diving activities to keep you entertained on Friday afternoon.

sections.heading: Day 15: Departure
sections.text: Depart from the boat after breakfast or earlier, depending on your transfer time to the airport or hotel. Check out at 10 AM.

sections.heading: Marine Life:
sections.text: Experience the rich biodiversity of the Red Sea, where vibrant coral reefs, clear blue waters, and dramatic drop-offs host an abundance of marine life. Encounter schools of colorful reef fish, graceful manta rays, turtles, moray eels, and pelagic species such as reef sharks and hammerheads, all thriving in one of the world’s most spectacular diving regions. The last dive will be on the penultimate day of the trip. Divers are recommended to wait for 24 hours before flying after the last dive.

sections.heading: Fury Shoals: Diving Adventure and Wellness Escape in the Red Sea
sections.text: Set off with the Dune Liveaboard to discover the enchanting Fury Shoals, a collection of vibrant reefs in the southern Red Sea. Renowned for its colorful coral gardens, caves, and swim-throughs, Fury Shoals offers divers of all levels a captivating underwater experience. Dive sites like Sha’ab Claudia and Malahi are famous for their stunning coral formations, maze-like passages, and thriving marine life. Experience the magic of Sataya Reef (Dolphin Reef), where you have the rare chance to snorkel or dive with playful spinner dolphins in crystal-clear waters. The underwater terrain is filled with soft and hard corals, offering shelter to schools of fish, moray eels, and turtles. Explore the legendary Abu Galawa's caves and the Tien Hsing wreck, a sunken tugboat now home to an array of colorful marine species. Fury Shoals is perfect for those seeking both adventure and tranquility, with its diverse dive sites catering to different skill levels. From vibrant coral gardens to unique underwater structures and playful encounters with dolphins, this trip promises an unforgettable Red Sea adventure for all.

sections.heading: Day 3-5: Fury Shoals
sections.text: On the first day, enjoy an exciting dive outside the Sataya lagoon. On the second day, experience snorkeling with dolphins in their natural habitat. For the third day, it’s up to you—choose between swimming with dolphins again or trying an introduction dive to explore the underwater world. sections.heading: Day 6: Sheleneyat
sections.text: After breakfast, a dolphin excursion and a dive for certified divers will be organized. You will then sail approximately 5 to 6 hours north to reach the site of Sheleneyat. You can take a snorkeling hike along the reef. After dinner, time to party!

sections.text: At the crack of dawn, the boat will sail to the Marsa Alam area, where you will go diving or snorkeling on the two sites selected by your guide. You will arrive at the marina early in the afternoon. Your guide will tell you all about the leisure activities you can book in the Marsa Alam area to spend an entertaining Friday afternoon.

sections.heading: Day 8: Departure
sections.text: Departure from the boat will be after breakfast or according to your flight and transfer schedules to the airport or hotel. Check out at 10 AM.

sections.text: Spinner dolphins, turtles, moray eels, reef sharks, and large schools of colorful reef fish are commonly seen around the vibrant coral gardens and reef systems of Fury Shoals in the southern Red Sea. sections.heading: Golden Triangle: Discover the Best of the Red Sea
sections.text: Embark on an unforgettable adventure with the Dune Liveaboard as you dive into the wonders of the Red Sea’s "Golden Triangle”. Begin with the Brother Islands, which offer some of the most thrilling dive sites in the Red Sea. Big Brother is famed for its dramatic walls covered with soft corals, gorgonians, and anemones, along with encounters with oceanic whitetips, hammerheads, and grey reef sharks. Divers can also explore the wrecks of the Aida and Numidia, now vibrant with marine life. Next, Daedalus Reef, a remote diving haven famous for its dramatic drop-offs, vibrant coral walls, and thrilling encounters with hammerhead sharks, oceanic whitetips, and manta rays, offers unmatched experiences for advanced divers. Conclude with Elphinstone Reef, renowned for its steep walls covered in soft corals and gorgonians, where encounters with reef sharks, barracudas, and dolphins are frequent. Known for its exhilarating currents and the iconic blue hole, Elphinstone provides a dynamic underwater experience that is both challenging and rewarding.

sections.heading: This diving safari takes you to discover the most famous Egyptian dive sites.
sections.text: You will make fabulous dives on the most legendary sites of Egypt. The name Golden Triangle refers to the geographical position of the dive sites that will be visited during the cruise, placed in the shape of a triangle.

sections.heading: These three dive sites are :
sections.text: the Brothers Islands, Daedalus Reef and Elphinstone Reef, ...hence the acronym BDE.

sections.heading: The Brothers Islands
sections.text: are two islands located 60 km off the coast of Al Qseir in Egyptian territorial waters. These islands are made of volcanic rocks. Big Brother is approximately 600m long and topped by a lighthouse built by the British in the 19th century. 4 keepers ensure the lighthouse operates properly and will be happy to welcome you for a visit. In the north of the island are 2 beautiful wrecks that you can discover during your dives: the Numidia (1901) is lying almost vertically against the reef between 10m and 83m and is covered with colorful corals. The Aida II (1958), a military ship supplying the Brothers Islands and bringing the new lighthouse keepers, sank 100m away from the Numidia and lay between 10m and 63m. In this area, you can have the opportunity to encounter a thresher shark... Small Brother is about 200m long. You will see, among other things, a beautiful garden of gorgonian sea fans, black corals, and many pelagic fishes.

sections.heading: Daedalus Reef
sections.text: is 600m long and 300m wide. It lies about 90km off the coast, south of Marsa Alam. It is topped by a lighthouse built by the French in 1863 and modified by the British in 1931. It is also possible to visit the lighthouse and enjoy its breathtaking view of the magnificent reef of Daedalus. At least ten different dives can be organized on this reef that has the greatest coral diversity in the Egyptian Red Sea. North of the reef, a school of hammerhead sharks is very often seen. A large number of pelagic fishes and varied fauna will enhance your dives.

sections.heading: Elphinstone
sections.text: is 400m long and 30m wide. Strong currents hit the northern and southern plateau bringing nutrients to a vast colony of soft corals. Many shark species, among which the oceanic white tip shark (Carcharhinus longimanus) are seen in the area. Let yourself be carried away by the currents and enjoy the abundant pelagic fauna. sections.heading: Mixed South, Egypt: A Journey Through the Best of the Red Sea
sections.text: Embark on a thrilling adventure with the Dune Liveaboard to the Mixed South, Egypt, where you will explore some of the Red Sea’s most iconic dive sites: Daedalus, Rocky, Zabargad, and Saint John’s. Start at Daedalus Reef, a remote site known for its stunning drop-offs, vibrant coral walls, and encounters with hammerhead sharks, oceanic whitetips, and manta rays. This dive site offers a truly exhilarating experience for advanced divers. Continue to the dramatic landscapes of Rocky Island and Zabargad Island, both surrounded by steep walls covered in colorful corals and frequented by reef sharks, moray eels, and schools of barracudas. Zabargad, with its turquoise lagoons and unique rock formations, also offers an intriguing underwater labyrinth to explore. Finally, dive into the wonders of Saint John’s, a vast network of reefs featuring an extraordinary diversity of marine life, from vibrant coral gardens to caves and tunnels. Whether you are navigating through the maze-like passages of Habili Ali or drifting along the walls of Gotta Kebir, Saint John’s promises a captivating underwater adventure that will leave every diver wanting more.

sections.heading: Day 3: Daedalus
sections.text: At sunrise, you will start your day of diving at the Daedalus Falls. Your guide will suggest three dives. This reef offers you ten different dives. You will make 2 dives north of the reef for perhaps the chance to observe hammerhead sharks. In the afternoon, you will dive west of the reef, where the coral diversity is impressive. This slope also offers perfect light in the afternoon. Between dives, you will have the opportunity to visit the Daedalus lighthouse. In the early evening, after dinner, the boat will continue its journey all night south to arrive in the early morning under the Tropic of Cancer at Rocky Island and Zabargad.

sections.heading: Day 4: Rocky and Zabargad Islands
sections.text: You will make three dives around the Rocky and Zabargad islands. The navigation times between the sites vary from 30 to 45 minutes between the islands. The dive sites are carefully chosen by your guide depending on the weather and the number of boats on the sites.

sections.heading: Day 5: St John's
sections.text: In the early morning, the captain and his crew will take you to the Saint John's sites. Three dives will be offered to you. The dive sites are carefully chosen by your guide depending on the weather and the number of boats on the sites.

sections.heading: Day 6: Fury Shoals and Sheleneyat
sections.text: That day, we will start the ascent to the north. On the way, we will stop at Sataya (Dolphin house) located in the Fury Shoals area, where you may have the opportunity to swim with the dolphins. We will then continue our ascent to the Sheleneyat site in the Wadi Gemal area, where the third dive of the day will take place at dusk or at night.

sections.text: In the early morning, you will arrive in the Marsa Alam area, on the mythical Elphinstone Reef. sections.heading: North Dahab Tiran: Discover Egypt’s Northern Red Sea Wonders
sections.text: Join the Dune Liveaboard for an adventure to North Dahab Tiran, known for its rich marine life and breathtaking dive sites. Begin at Dahab’s famous Blue Hole and Canyon, where you will explore stunning vertical walls and deep caverns suited for divers of all levels. Next, venture to the Straits of Tiran, featuring four reefs—Jackson, Woodhouse, Thomas, and Gordon—famous for their dramatic drop-offs, swift currents, and crystal-clear waters. These sites offer thrilling encounters with reef sharks, eagle rays, and vibrant fish schools, perfect for drift diving. Conclude your journey at Ras Mohammed National Park, where you'll discover colorful coral gardens, swim-throughs, and walls teeming with diverse marine life. Each dive promises a unique and unforgettable experience in Egypt’s northern Red Sea.

You will then dive at Jackson Reef, followed by a dive at Gordon Reef. Afterward, you will head towards Ras Abou Gallum.

sections.heading: Day 4: Dahab and Nabq
sections.text: Explore the wonders of Dahab and Nabq, two iconic diving spots in Sinai. In Dahab, dive the Blue Hole and Canyon, known for dramatic drop-offs and vibrant marine life. Nabq offers tranquil waters, coral plateaus, and mangroves, with turtles and rays for all-level divers.

sections.heading: Day 5: Ras Mohamed and the Thistlegorm
sections.text: Discover the best of Ras Mohamed and the Thistlegorm, two iconic Red Sea dive sites. Ras Mohamed offers vibrant coral reefs, dramatic walls, and abundant marine life, making it a must-see for divers. At the Thistlegorm, explore the legendary WWII shipwreck, filled with fascinating artifacts and surrounded by schools of fish, creating a perfect mix of history and underwater adventure.

sections.heading: Day 6: Thistlegorm and Abu Nuhas
sections.text: Dive into history and beauty at Thistlegorm and Abu Nuhas, two legendary Red Sea sites. Thistlegorm, a WWII shipwreck, reveals fascinating artifacts and vibrant marine life. Abu Nuhas, the "Shipwreck Graveyard," offers stunning dives on multiple wrecks, each teeming with fish and coral, blending adventure with underwater exploration.

dune-longara::North Ras Mohammed (Safaga.intro: Join the Dune Liveaboard for an exhilarating adventure exploring the best of North Ras Mohamed, a region celebrated for its incredible dive sites and rich marine biodiversity. This itinerary takes you to some of the Red Sea’s most iconic locations, from vibrant coral gardens to historical shipwrecks teeming with life. Begin your journey with an unforgettable dive at the legendary Thistlegorm wreck, one of the most famous dive sites in the world. This sunken World War II ship is an underwater museum filled with artifacts, trucks, motorcycles, and weapons, now covered with colorful corals and surrounded by schools of jacks, barracudas, and batfish. Continue to Ras Mohamed National Park, where you’ll explore stunning dive sites like Shark Reef and Yolanda Reef, renowned for their dramatic coral walls, diverse marine life, and crystal-clear waters.

sections.heading: North Tiran: Explore the Wonders of the Red Sea
sections.text: Set sail with the Dune Liveaboard for an unforgettable adventure in North Tiran, one of the Red Sea’s premier diving destinations. This journey will take you to some of the most spectacular dive sites around the Straits of Tiran, where vibrant marine life and breathtaking underwater landscapes await. Begin your exploration with dives at Jackson Reef, a world-renowned site known for its strong currents, incredible visibility, and sightings of hammerhead sharks, eagle rays, and large schools of barracudas. Continue to Thomas Reef, a dive site celebrated for its deep canyons, coral plateaus, and the chance to encounter whitetip reef sharks and other pelagic species, and Gordon Reef, famous for its coral gardens, large gorgonian fans, and the wreck of the Loullia. Then, dive into Ras Mohammed National Park, where you'll discover colorful coral gardens, swim-throughs, and walls teeming with diverse marine life. Each dive promises a unique and unforgettable experience in Egypt’s northern Red Sea.

sections.heading: Hidden Treasures of the Red Sea: Dive into St. John’s Reef
sections.text: Set out on an extraordinary journey with the Dune Liveaboard to explore the captivating underwater world of St. John’s Reef, located in the southern Red Sea near Marsa Alam. Dive into the pristine waters of this remote dive site, renowned for its stunning drop-offs, vibrant coral gardens, and incredible diversity of marine life. Discover the hidden gems of Egypt’s underwater paradise, where encounters with hammerhead sharks, dolphins, and large pelagic fish are just a few of the thrilling experiences that await. At St. John’s Reef, immerse yourself in some of the Red Sea’s most iconic dive spots, such as Habili Ali, Gotta Kebir, and Dangerous Reef. These sites offer a mesmerizing array of coral formations, from steep walls adorned with soft corals to expansive plateaus teeming with reef fish, barracudas, and colorful anthias. The area is also known for its remarkable underwater caves and tunnels, providing a unique diving experience unlike any other in Egypt. This adventure promises divers a captivating exploration of St. John’s Reef, where each dive unveils a new chapter in the Red Sea’s vibrant underwater world, offering both serenity and excitement for divers of all levels.

sections.heading: Ultra South Reef Elba: Discover Egypt’s Hidden Red Sea Treasures
sections.text: Join the Dune Liveaboard for an unforgettable journey to Ultra South Reef Elba, diving into Egypt’s most untouched sites. Begin at Daedalus Reef, famed for its dramatic drop-offs, vibrant coral walls, and encounters with hammerhead sharks, oceanic whitetips, and manta rays—perfect for experienced divers. Continue to the Rocky and Zabargad Islands, where steep coral-covered walls attract reef sharks, moray eels, and barracudas. Zabargad’s turquoise lagoons and unique rock formations create an intriguing underwater playground with labyrinthine passages. Then discover the unspoilt reefs of Elba, with its mythical wreck Di Levanzo! You'll discover unspoilt sites in a little-visited area that will give you the impression of being alone in the world. Finish at Saint John’s, a network of reefs offering impressive biodiversity, colourful coral gardens, and exciting tunnels. Drift along the walls of Gotta Kebir for an adventure that will leave you in awe of the beauty of the Red Sea. An experience that will leave every diver with unforgettable memories of Egypt’s underwater wonders.

sections.text: Early in the morning, you will perform your first dive at Ras Abou Gallum. Three dives are offered in this protected area, teeming with life. The first dive will be on a drop-off, followed by two more dives in magnificent coral gardens.

sections.heading: Day 5: Dahab
sections.text: On the fifth day of the cruise, you will have the opportunity to explore the internationally renowned diving and snorkeling site, the Blue Hole in Dahab. Afterward, you will dive at a site known as the Canyon, followed by a third dive at the Island, a stunning coral garden that is sure to amaze you.

sections.heading: Day 6: Ras Mohamed and Thistlegorm
sections.text: At dawn, the boat will head towards Ras Mohamed Marine Park where you will dive twice on the breathtaking drop-offs, surrounded by thousands of colorful fish. After lunch, the boat will travel northwest. The third dive of the day will take place at the legendary wreck of the SS Thistlegorm, discovered by Cousteau in the 1950s.

sections.heading: Day 7: Thistlegorm and Gubal
sections.text: Today, you will dive at least twice on the wreck of the SS Thistlegorm. Then, you will sail for two hours across the Strait of Gubal to reach the small island of Gubal, where you will make the third dive of the day.

sections.heading: Day 8: Abu Nuhas and Hurghada
sections.text: In the morning, you will conduct your first two dives on wrecks. After lunch, the captain and his crew will take you further south towards Hurghada, where you will perform the third dive of the day. Depending on demand, your guide may organize a night dive. The boat will moor behind a reef for the night to stay sheltered from the waves. This schedule may be modified by your guide depending on weather conditions.

sections.heading: Day 9: Brothers
sections.text: Having arrived at the site the previous evening, you will carry out three dives throughout the day on the stunning drop-offs of the Brothers islands. Due to new regulations aimed at protecting the marine ecosystem, cruise boats are now only allowed to spend one day at the Brothers Islands. Therefore, the boat will then sail overnight to Daedalus, arriving in the early morning.

sections.heading: Day 10: Daedalus
sections.text: Three dives are offered at the Daedalus site, a potential meeting place with hammerhead sharks. A visit to the lighthouse may be organized by your guide, depending on agreements with the local keepers.

sections.heading: Day 11: Rocky Zabargad
sections.text: You will perform three dives around the Rocky and Zabargad islands. The navigation time between sites varies from 30 to 45 minutes. Dive sites are carefully selected by your guide based on the weather and the number of boats at each site.

sections.heading: Day 12: St. John’s
sections.text: Early in the morning, the captain and his crew will take you to the dive sites at St. John's. Three dives are planned for the day. The navigation times between sites in the St. John's area vary between 30 minutes, and 1 hour and 30 minutes. Dive sites are carefully chosen by your guide based on the weather conditions and the number of boats present.

sections.heading: Day 13: Fury Shoals & Sheleneyat
sections.text: Today, we begin our journey northward. En route, we will stop at Sataya (Dolphin House) located in the Fury Shoals area, where you may have the opportunity to swim with dolphins. We will then continue north to the Sheleneyat site in the Wadi Gemal area, where the third dive of the day will take place at twilight or night.

sections.heading: Day 14: Elphinstone Reef
sections.text: In the early morning, you will arrive in the Marsa Alam area, at the legendary Elphinstone Reef. You will conduct two dives there, before sailing for another two hours to reach Port Ghalib Marina in the early afternoon. You can use the rear platform to rinse your gear. Your guide will also offer various non-diving activities to keep you entertained on Friday afternoon.

sections.heading: Day 15: Departure
sections.text: Depart from the boat after breakfast or earlier depending on your transfer time to the airport or hotel. (*) the itinerary description provided by the boat operator. The last dive will be on the penultimate day of the trip. Divers are recommended to wait for 24 hours before flying after the last dive.
